CausalChain: Chronic liver inflammation -> Activation of CAFs and alteration of LSECs -> Secretion of immunomodulatory cytokines (e.g., IL-6, CXCL11) and growth factors -> Tumor cells increase production of immunosuppressive metabolites (kynurenine, SAM, MTA) -> Upregulation of PD-1, CTLA-4 on T lymphocytes and heightened PD-L1 expression by LSECs -> Induction of T cell exhaustion and dampening of cytotoxic responses -> The immunosuppressive TME supports tumor progression
Hypothesis: Inhibiting the metabolic pathways responsible for the production of immunosuppressive metabolites (such as kynurenine, SAM, and MTA) in HCC cells will reprogram the tumor microenvironment, restore T cell functionality, and synergize with PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint blockade to improve therapeutic outcomes in hepatocellular carcinoma.
Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) develops within a uniquely immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) that is shaped not only by inflammatory cytokines and immune checkpoint signals but also by metabolic reprogramming. The interplay between cancer‐associated fibroblasts (CAFs), hepatocytes, liver sinusoidal endothelial cells (LSECs), and immune cells drives the production of immunosuppressive metabolites such as kynurenine, S‐adenosylmethionine (SAM), and methylthioadenosine (MTA). These metabolites have been implicated in upregulating inhibitory receptors on T lymphocytes, thereby promoting T cell exhaustion and undermining anti‐tumor immunity. The reprogramming of non‐immune cells, especially LSECs, further reinforces immune tolerance via increased PD‐L1 expression. Together, these mechanisms support tumor growth and resistance to standard immunotherapies. This review proposes the therapeutic potential of intervening in the metabolic crosstalk that drives immune suppression in HCC.
